Research, explained

Fourteen projects about helping phones understand indoor spaces, keeping AI dependable when conditions change, and turning raw signals into useful decisions.

2026Continual federated learning

ARMOR

ARMOR uses a dual-AI architecture: one AI handles mobile indoor localization while a second AI watches how the first one learns. When cyberattacks or faulty updates push the locator off course, the guardian detects the error and corrects the learning process before the shared model is damaged.

Read the paper ↗
2025Graph attention

GATE

Wi-Fi measurements do not behave like tidy coordinates, and two phones can hear the same room differently. GATE treats access points and locations as a living graph, then rebuilds the useful connections in real time so the model can pay attention to the relationships that still make sense.

Read the paper ↗
2025Explainable AI

LogNet: explainable indoor localization

A neural network can give a location without showing why. LogNet translates that decision into simple logic-like rules, revealing which Wi-Fi access points mattered, which ones were unreliable, and how changes in the building affected the answer—while also making the model smaller and faster.

Read the paper ↗
2025Domain-incremental learning

DAILOC

A location system should not confuse “this is a different phone” or “the building changed this month” with “the user moved.” DAILOC separates those kinds of change from the clues that actually identify a place, then uses a small memory of earlier lessons so learning something new does not erase what worked before.

Read the paper ↗
2025Class-incremental learning

CIELO

When a building map expands, a model must learn new rooms without forgetting the old ones or storing every past Wi-Fi sample. CIELO keeps a compact set of representative memories and uses crowdsourced observations to add locations gradually, saving storage and reducing the “forgetting” that often follows new training.

View the publication record ↗
2025Secure federated learning

SAFELOC

Federated learning protects raw phone data, but attackers can still send poisoned training examples. SAFELOC uses one compact network to both estimate location and spot suspicious data, then changes how strongly each phone’s update influences the shared model according to the risk it detects.

Read the paper ↗
2024Adversarial resilience

SENTINEL

A rogue Wi-Fi access point can alter the signal pattern and trick a phone into reporting the wrong place. SENTINEL uses capsule networks—small groups of neurons that preserve relationships between clues—to recognize trustworthy patterns even when devices differ, signals drift, or an attacker interferes.

Read the paper ↗
2024Curriculum adversarial learning

CALLOC

Instead of exposing a model to every possible attack at once, CALLOC teaches it in a curriculum: begin with easier disruptions, then increase the difficulty as the model learns. A lightweight attention system makes that security training practical on resource-limited phones.

Read the paper ↗
2023Contrastive learning

STELLAR

Two phones—and the same phone months apart—can record different Wi-Fi values in the exact same spot. STELLAR trains twin neural networks to recognize which fingerprints should count as “the same place,” allowing the system to stay accurate across devices and over time without repeated recalibration.

Read the paper ↗
2023Privacy-preserving learning

FedHIL

FedHIL lets many phones improve one indoor-location model while keeping their original Wi-Fi readings on-device. It selectively adjusts the parts of the shared model that need help, so unusually noisy phones do not erase useful knowledge gathered from the rest.

Read the paper ↗
2023Vision transformers

VITAL

VITAL arranges a phone’s Wi-Fi fingerprint so a vision transformer can examine it like a set of related image patches. The model compares distant parts of the signal pattern at once, helping it find place-specific structure that remains useful even when different phone hardware changes the raw measurements.

Read the paper ↗
2023Compact hybrid learning

SANGRIA

SANGRIA first compresses a large Wi-Fi fingerprint into a smaller set of useful features, then passes those features to a team of decision trees that correct one another’s mistakes. The combination reduces noise from different devices while keeping the location estimate efficient.

Read the paper ↗
2022Multi-head attention

Smartphone-invariant localization

Different phone radios can distort Wi-Fi strength in different ways. This work gives the model several “attention heads,” each free to focus on a different group of access points, so together they can find the stable parts of a fingerprint and locate a user more consistently across devices.

Read the paper ↗
2020Ground-penetrating radar

Underground object size approximation

Ground-penetrating radar sends energy into the soil and records the returning echoes. This project processes those signals as images, isolates the curved reflection left by a buried object, and uses its shape to estimate the object’s size before anyone digs.
